title: Atapa
author: Laker Grace
desc: Stiff sorghum porridge mingled until it leaves the stick clean, eaten once a day at sunset with bush greens and groundnut paste — the Karamojong and Teso staple.
longDesc: Atapa is the stiff sorghum porridge of Karamoja, also made with millet and in Teso usually cut with cassava flour. It is eaten once daily at sunset, which is the pastoral pattern rather than a preference, and it goes with bush greens and groundnut paste. Karamoja is the worst-documented food region in Uganda by a wide margin — dish names exist and methods do not — so the mingling method here follows karo, the one Ugandan mingled-flour staple that is written down with quantities.
ingredients: Cassava flour, in the Teso version, to cut the sorghum
// No quantities are documented for atapa. The karo ratio, 3 litres of water to a kilo of flour, is the nearest documented guide
steps: Bring the water to the boil.
Add the flour gradually while stirring continuously, to prevent air pockets.
Work it until the water has reduced, then add more hot water — never cold, which sets the flour stiff.
Keep mingling until the mixture no longer sticks to the stirring stick.
Turn it out, shape it, cover it and rest it briefly before serving.
Serve with bush greens and groundnut paste.
chefTips: No longer sticking to the stick. That is the cue for every mingled starch in Uganda and atapa is no exception.
Hot water for any addition after the first. Cold water at that stage stiffens the flour and the batch is finished.
Add the flour gradually. Dumped in it traps air pockets you cannot work out.

Be honest about the sourcing here: no method or quantities for atapa exist in any source I could reach. The mingling technique is taken from karo, UGA091, which is the same class of dish and is documented with quantities. That is a cross-reference, not an attestation, and you should know which is which.
In Teso, atapa is usually cut with cassava flour, exactly as karo is — the cassava makes a coarse flour workable.
Eaten once daily at sunset in the pastoral pattern. That is not a serving suggestion, it is how Karamoja eats.
Bush greens and groundnut paste are the documented accompaniments.

The single useful published treatment of Karamojong food is the Eating with Africa cookbook's Karamoja chapter, and neither its authors nor any named Karamojong cook is credited on the pages reachable online. That is a real problem with the record and not something I can fix from here.
commonMistakes: Adding the flour all at once.
Stopping before it leaves the stick clean.
Using sorghum flour alone where cassava is the local practice.
Treating it as a breakfast porridge — it is a stiff evening staple.
sources: The dish itself is documented as a stiff sorghum, sometimes millet, porridge served with bush greens and groundnut paste, eaten once daily at sunset in the pastoral pattern, with the Teso version usually cut with cassava flour. That comes from the Ngakarimojong and Ateso entries of the regional survey for this collection, drawing on Kara-Tunga's publications and the Eating with Africa cookbook, which is the only published treatment of Karamojong food and credits neither its authors nor any named Karamojong cook on its accessible pages.

No method, no quantities, no timings and no doneness cue for atapa exist in any source reached. The mingling method in the steps above is taken from the Ankole karo chapter of the Wikibooks project 'Mujje Tulye from Uganda', which documents the same class of dish with quantities — three litres of water to a kilo of flour, gradual flour addition to prevent air pockets, hot water only for later additions, and the no-longer-adheres-to-the-utensil cue. That is a cross-reference from a related dish and is labelled as such rather than presented as an attestation for atapa.
Karamoja is the worst-documented food region in Uganda: the Slow Food Uganda booklet, which is otherwise excellent, carries nothing on it at all.
storage: Best fresh. It firms considerably as it cools.
reheating: Steam briefly, or eat it cold.
healthBenefits: Sorghum is high in fibre, iron, magnesium and B vitamins, and is naturally gluten-free.
Drought-tolerant grain, which is why it anchors diets in Uganda's driest region.
Flour and water only — no fat at all.
Very filling, with a slow energy release suited to one meal a day.
culturalNote: One meal a day at sunset is a pastoral rhythm, not a hardship story, and atapa is built for it — dense, slow and eaten with whatever greens the bush has given. That Karamoja's foods are known by name and almost never by method is the largest single gap in the written record of Ugandan cooking.
